how-much-cash-do-i-need-for-net-30-payme.text:
← Subcontractor Cash Flow Planner

How much cash do you need for net 30, 45, 60, or 90 payment terms?

Payment terms are the single biggest lever in a subcontract's cash gap, because every extra day of terms is another day your materials and overhead sit unfunded. Here is the arithmetic on a $10,000 subcontract at five common terms, holding everything else — materials, weekly burn, retention, buffer, and starting cash — at the calculator's own defaults.

Cash needed and funding gap at five payment terms

$10,000 invoice, $2,500 materials, $700/week burn, 10% retention, 14-day late-payment buffer, $5,000 cash available. Arithmetic only — no recommendation.
Payment terms Expected payment day* Cash needed before payment Funding gap
Net 15Day 29$5,400$400
Net 30Day 44$6,900$1,900
Net 45Day 59$8,400$3,400
Net 60Day 74$9,900$4,900
Net 90Day 104$12,900$7,900

*Contract terms plus the calculator's 14-day late-payment buffer, which models the gap between "invoice due" and "invoice actually paid" that shows up across the trades even on paper-clean contracts.

Cash needed grows by exactly $700 for every extra 7 days of terms — that is the weekly burn rate doing the work, not the invoice size or retention, both of which are held constant across this table. The funding gap grows just as fast because starting cash ($5,000) does not move: each 15-day step from net 15 to net 90 adds roughly $1,500 to the gap.

The takeaway is not "avoid long terms" — longer terms are often non-negotiable on larger contracts. It is that the same $10,000 subcontract needs very different working capital depending on the terms alone, so the terms line in a contract is worth pricing into your cash plan before you sign, not after materials are already ordered.

Open the calculator and enter your own invoice, materials, burn rate, and terms to see your actual gap. Nothing you enter is uploaded.

This page is arithmetic, not legal, tax, financial, or accounting advice. It does not tell you what terms to accept or predict when a specific client will actually pay.

Common questions

How much cash do I need to carry a subcontract on net 30 payment terms?

It depends on your materials cost and weekly burn rate, not just the invoice size. On this calculator's own defaults — $2,500 in materials, $700 a week in overhead, a 14-day late-payment buffer on top of the 30-day terms — cash needed before payment works out to $6,900. Compared against $5,000 in cash available for the project, that is a $1,900 funding gap you would need to bridge with more starting cash, a materials deposit, progress billing, or a line of credit.

How much does the funding gap grow if payment terms stretch from net 30 to net 60 or net 90?

Roughly linearly with the extra weeks, because the calculator multiplies your weekly burn by the days until expected payment. Going from net 30 to net 60 on the same $10,000 subcontract raises cash needed from $6,900 to $9,900, and the funding gap from $1,900 to $4,900 — a $3,000 increase driven entirely by an extra 15 days (net 60 plus the same 14-day buffer versus net 30 plus that buffer) of overhead that has to be funded before the invoice pays. Net 90 terms nearly double cash needed again, to $12,900, for a $7,900 gap.

index.html.text:
Free working-capital check

Will the project pay before your cash runs out?

A payment-delay cash flow planner for independent subcontractors. Model the invoice, retention, materials, supplier terms, a deposit, and a realistic late-payment buffer before you order anything.

After using this, you can now see the cash a subcontract needs, what bridging it costs, and how much late payment it survives — which used to take a spreadsheet and a hopeful guess.

Your project

Scenario result

This is a timing scenario, not a prediction. The cost to bridge is simple daily interest on the shortfall, not a quote — it ignores draw fees, minimum charges, and whether credit is available to you at all. Confirm contract terms, retention release dates, taxes, debt, financing, and supplier requirements with your accountant or adviser.

Share link: your numbers ride in the page's own URL, never sent to a server — only share it with people you trust.

Privacy and limits

Everything runs in your browser. There are no accounts, cookies, analytics vendors, network requests, or uploads. Optional usage counters record only feature names in local storage, never your numbers or identity.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, financial, or accounting advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Common questions

What is the difference between "expected payment day" and when retention actually clears?

Expected payment day is contract terms plus your late-payment buffer — on the defaults, 30 days of terms + a 14-day buffer = day 44, when the collectable $9,000 (invoice less 10% retention) is expected to land. Retention release day adds the separate retention-release period on top of that — 44 + 60 = day 104 — because retention on most construction contracts is held until a milestone like project close-out or a warranty period, well after the regular invoice pays.

How is "cash needed before payment" calculated?

Materials and upfront costs, plus your weekly burn rate stretched across the days until expected payment — on the defaults, $2,500 materials + $700/week × (44 days ÷ 7) ≈ $2,500 + $4,400 = $6,900. That weekly-burn term is what most spreadsheet estimates skip: it is not just materials that need funding, it is every day of overhead and other bills that keep running while you wait to be paid. See how that cash-needed figure changes at net 15, 30, 45, 60, and 90 payment terms.

What does the funding gap actually mean, and what closes it?

Cash needed minus cash available for the project, floored at zero — on the defaults, $6,900 needed − $5,000 available = a $1,900 gap. Four of the things that close it are fields you can turn here: a deposit or mobilisation payment (25% of this invoice closes it outright), supplier terms that outlast the client's payment date, a shorter payment-terms negotiation, or more starting cash. A smaller late-payment buffer closes it on paper too — only do that if you have a real reason to trust this client. Whatever is left after those is a line of credit sized to at least the gap, and the planner prices that.

My supply house gives me 30 days — why didn't that close the gap?

Because the client pays later than the supplier does. On the defaults you are paid on day 44 and a net-30 materials invoice falls due on day 30, so the $2,500 still leaves your account first: supplier terms shorten the borrowing window (you run short on day 30 rather than day 26) without changing what the job needs. Set supplier terms to 45 and the answer flips — the bill is due after the client's money lands, the materials never need bridging, and the $1,900 gap disappears. The lever is not the length of the terms, it is whether they outlast the client.

The gap is $1,900. Is that a reason to turn the job down?

Not on its own — the size of a gap and the cost of a gap are different numbers. On the defaults you are short from day 26 to day 44, and the shortfall ramps up across those 18 days rather than sitting at $1,900 the whole time, so carrying it on a 12% line of credit costs around $6. The real questions are whether you can reach $1,900 at all, and what the same gap costs when the client stretches to net 90. That interest figure is simple daily interest on the daily shortfall and ignores draw fees, minimum charges, and factoring discounts — treat it as a floor, not a quote.

How many days late can the client pay before I am actually in trouble?

That is the “late payment you can still absorb” line, and it appears once the scenario is covered. It counts the extra days of slip — beyond the buffer you already entered — that your remaining cash and weekly burn survive. On the defaults with a 25% deposit you hold $600 spare against $100 a day of burn, so six days. It can read zero even with money left over: if the materials invoice falls due the day after payment was expected, one day of slip pulls that whole bill in ahead of the money, and the planner shows you that cliff instead of the comfortable-looking surplus.

Why include a late-payment buffer at all if the contract says net 30?

Because contract terms describe when payment is owed, not when it reliably arrives. A 14-day buffer on the default scenario models the gap between "invoice due" and "invoice actually paid" that shows up across the trades when a client's own approval or AP cycle runs slow. Set it to zero only if you have direct evidence this particular client always pays on the contract date.

Is retention money gone, or does it show up somewhere in the plan?

It is deferred, not lost. The retained amount ($1,000 on the default $10,000 invoice at 10%) is shown separately with its own expected release day, so it never inflates the cash the project planner assumes you'll have on the regular payment date. Treat retention release as a second, later collection date with its own risk of slipping, not as part of day-44 cash.

Once I know the gap, how do I actually close it?

This planner sizes the gap and prices what carrying it costs at a rate you choose — it does not lend money. See how this compares to Billd, a real material-financing product that pays your supplier directly and lets you repay over up to 120 days, for one way to actually close a gap once you know its size. If your own back-of-envelope plan books materials as cash out the moment you order, see why that can overstate the gap by the entire amount.

Is my project data uploaded anywhere?

No. There are no accounts, cookies, analytics vendors, or network requests — the scenario runs entirely in your browser, "Save locally" keeps a draft in this browser's storage, and CSV export saves a file straight to your device. Anonymous feature counts can be turned off with the checkbox in the Privacy and limits section above.

Tracking retainage withheld on a signed contract rather than the whole job's cash timing? The construction retainage calculator models the hold, release, and carrying cost — nothing uploaded.

Subcontractor Cash Flow Planner is free to use. Optional support: GitHub Sponsors. Keep a copy of important project assumptions outside this browser.

vs-billd.html.text:
← Subcontractor Cash Flow Planner

Subcontractor Cash Flow Planner vs. Billd Material Financing

Billd is a real financing product for commercial subcontractors: it pays your material supplier directly and lets you repay Billd over up to 120 days — or whenever your GC pays you, whichever comes first — subject to credit approval. This calculator is not a lender. It is a free page that answers the question you would want answered before applying anywhere: does this project actually create a funding gap, how big is it, and what would it cost to carry?

What each one actually is

QuestionBilldThis calculator
What is itA financing company: it pays your supplier, you repay Billd on terms.A free, static calculator. No lending, no account.
Does it lend moneyYes, real credit, subject to underwriting and approval.No. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type in.
Published costStandard fee of 2.99% per month on the amount financed, plus a 2% purchase fee typically offset by a supplier cash discount; no monthly or annual account fee; no penalty for paying early.Free. You choose the borrowing rate to model — the calculator does not set or charge one.
EligibilityPublished minimums for its term-loan/credit-line products: $100,000+ annual revenue, 1+ year in business, 625+ credit score.None. No revenue minimum, no credit check, no account.
SetupOnline enrollment in about 5 minutes; approval in as little as 24 hours, per Billd.Instant — open the page and type numbers.
What it coversFinancing the material purchase itself, for up to 120 days.Deposit timing, retention, supplier terms, weekly burn, and a chosen borrowing rate — the full shape of the gap, not just the materials line.
Where your data goesBusiness and credit information submitted for underwriting.Nowhere. Runs in your browser; nothing is uploaded.

Facts on Billd sourced from Billd's own material financing, finance-charge estimate, and FAQ pages. Verify current terms directly with Billd before relying on any of them — pricing is subject to credit approval and may change.

Using them together

This calculator's own default scenario — a $10,000 invoice, $2,500 in materials, $700/week burn, net-30 terms, 10% retention, and a 14-day late-payment buffer — produces a $1,900 funding gap. At a 12% borrowing rate the calculator prices carrying that gap at about $6.25. Billd's published standard fee, 2.99% a month, works out to about 35.9% if you annualize it by simple multiplication (2.99 × 12). Typing that figure into the “Rate on money you borrow to bridge” field here prices the same $1,900 gap at roughly $18.68 — a rough translation of Billd's monthly rate into this calculator's field, not a quote from Billd. Billd's real fee applies to the material purchase amount over its own weekly repayment schedule, not to this calculator's day-by-day shortfall model, so treat the $18.68 figure as a way to compare orders of magnitude, not as what Billd would actually charge you.

The two tools answer different halves of the same decision. This calculator tells you whether a gap exists and roughly what it costs to carry at any rate you enter — useful before you apply anywhere. Billd is one real way to actually close a materials-funding gap once you know it is there and decide financing is worth its published fee.

Size your own gap first

Common questions

Does Billd replace this calculator, or does this calculator replace Billd?

Neither — they answer different questions. Billd is a construction-material financing company: it pays your supplier directly and lets you repay Billd over up to 120 days, or whenever your GC pays you, whichever is sooner, subject to credit approval. This calculator does not lend anything. It is a free, no-account page that tells you whether a project creates a funding gap in the first place, how big it is, and what it would cost to carry at a rate you choose. Knowing the size and cost of the gap is useful before deciding whether financing it — through Billd, a bank line, or your own cash — is worth it.

What does Billd cost, and can I model that cost here?

Per Billd's own published pricing, its standard fee is 2.99% per month on the amount financed, plus a 2% purchase fee Billd says is typically offset by a supplier cash discount, with no monthly or annual account fee to enroll and no penalty for paying early. 2.99% a month works out to about 35.9% if annualized by simple multiplication (2.99 × 12) — not a quote, since Billd's real pricing is credit-based and applies to its own weekly repayment schedule rather than this calculator's day-by-day shortfall model, but close enough to type into the “Rate on money you borrow to bridge (APR %)” field here to see roughly what carrying your own gap at a similar rate would look like.

Who can actually use Billd?

Billd's published minimums for its term-loan and credit-line products are $100,000+ in annual revenue, at least one year in business, and a 625+ credit score, and enrolling means submitting business and credit information for underwriting — about five minutes online, with approval in as little as 24 hours per Billd. This calculator has no eligibility bar at all: no revenue minimum, no credit check, no account, because it doesn't extend credit — it does the arithmetic on numbers you type in, and nothing you enter leaves your browser.

Is this page affiliated with Billd?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Billd, LLC. BILLD and the BILLD logo are trademarks of Billd, LLC, named here only to describe a real financing service this calculator's output can help you evaluate.

vs-treating-materials-as-cash-out-on-day.text:
← Subcontractor Cash Flow Planner

Subcontractor Cash Flow Planner vs. treating materials as cash out on day one

The safe-sounding way to budget a job is to book the materials cost as cash out the moment you order — it feels conservative. Most subs do not actually pay a supply house on the spot; they buy on an account with net terms. Whether that due date lands before or after the client pays decides whether the materials line needs bridging at all, and a plan that assumes day-zero cash out cannot tell you which.

Same materials line, two different real answers

On this calculator's own default scenario — a $10,000 invoice, $2,500 in materials, $700/week burn, net-30 client terms, 10% retention, a 14-day late-payment buffer, and $5,000 starting cash — the client is expected to pay on day 44.

How the $2,500 materials purchase is financedCash needed before paymentFunding gap
Booked as cash out on day one (the back-of-envelope assumption)$6,900$1,900
Supply-house account, net 30 (due day 30, before the client pays)$6,900 — unchanged$1,900 — unchanged
Supply-house account, net 45 (due day 45, one day after the client pays)$4,400$0
 Figures from this calculator's own planCashflow(), not hand-typed.

The net-30 account changes nothing, because its due date still falls before the client's expected payment — you are still funding the materials out of pocket, just for a shorter window than a true day-zero purchase. The net-45 account is due one day after the client pays, so the client's own money covers the materials purchase and the entire funding gap disappears. Same $2,500 line, same kind of supplier relationship, opposite answer — decided by a single day on one invoice due date most back-of-envelope plans never look up.

Enter your own supplier terms

Why the naive assumption is not "conservative"

Treating a materials purchase as immediate cash out reads as the safe, pessimistic choice — if anything, you would expect it to overstate the gap rather than get it wrong in a way that matters. But "overstate by how much" is exactly the part a day-zero assumption cannot answer, and on this scenario the overstatement is the entire gap: $1,900 that a supplier account already due after the client pays would never actually need funding. A cash plan that books materials on day zero cannot distinguish a real $1,900 shortfall from a $0 one that only looks like $1,900 because the supplier's own terms were never priced in.

This is not a claim that supplier credit is free or that you should take it — a supply-house account may carry fees, limits, or terms this calculator does not model, and the payment-terms side of the gap still needs sizing on its own. It is a claim about sizing: whichever way you finance materials, the one date that decides whether it matters is the supplier's due date against the client's expected payment day, and a day-zero assumption throws that date away before you ever get to compare it.

Common questions

Why does assuming materials are cash out on day one overstate the funding gap?

Because most subs do not pay a supply house on the spot -- they buy on an account with net terms, commonly net 30 or net 45. If that due date falls after the client's expected payment, the client's money covers the materials before the supplier ever collects, and the materials line needs no bridging at all. Treating the purchase as day-zero cash out, as a back-of-envelope plan usually does, prices a gap that may not exist.

Why doesn't every supplier account close the gap the same way?

Because it is a race between two dates, not a feature of having terms at all. On this calculator's own default scenario the client is expected to pay on day 44. A net-30 supplier account is due on day 30 -- still before the client pays -- so the requirement is completely unchanged at $6,900 and the $1,900 gap stands. A net-45 account is due on day 45, one day after the client's payment lands, so the materials never need bridging and the gap closes to $0. Same $2,500 materials line, same supplier relationship in spirit, opposite answer, decided by a single day.

Is a supplier account always better than paying cash for materials?

Not necessarily -- this page is not a recommendation to use supplier credit, only a correction to a sizing assumption. A supply-house account may carry its own fees, credit limits, or relationship terms this calculator does not model. What it does show is that the naive day-zero assumption is not a conservative simplification, it is a specific and sometimes large overstatement, and the size of the overstatement depends on one date you would not otherwise think to check.
